dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our word page. This page teaches you the words of Unit 1, "Welcome to School" — words like table, chair, crayon and hello. We learn words by hearing them, saying them, and using them, so they stay in your head. You will need your voice, your eyes, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are 8 steps, and there are 67 words to learn — we do one word at a time, so there is no rush. Let's start! 1. Look at the left side of your screen. That is your word list. Press the first word. A card opens with everything about that word. I expect you to press just one word and look at its card. Good — that is your word for now. 2. Now press Hear it. Listen carefully. Then say the word out loud with your own mouth. Next press Again and say it one more time. I expect to hear your voice, not a quiet mouth! Say it with me, slowly. 3. Now read the meaning on the card. Press the little speaker next to it to hear the meaning read to you. Then tell me what the word means in your own words. It does not have to be perfect. I expect a try, like "a chair is a thing I sit on."

4. Look at the part called In a sentence. Read the first sentence. Press Hear sentence to listen to it. Use the arrows to move through every sentence on the card. Then pick one sentence and read it out loud yourself. I expect you to hear all of them and read one aloud. 5. Now look at Spelling. See the letters of the word. Say each letter one by one, slowly, like this: c... h... a... i... r. Then say the whole word again. I expect neat, slow letters — not fast ones. 6. Now it is your turn to write. In the box, type a sentence with your word. The grey words help you start. Then press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you and fix anything it points out. I expect one short sentence that makes sense, like "This is a chair." Say it out loud first, then write it. 7. Can you say the word? Do you know what it means? Did you write a sentence? Then press I know this word. Your word gets a LEARNED tag in the list. I expect you to press it only when all three are true — that is being honest, and honest learners learn fastest. 8. Now press the next word in your list. Do the same steps again: Hear it, Again, meaning, sentences, spelling, your own sentence, then I know this word. One word at a time, over and over. You will know the page is finished when every word in the list has a LEARNED tag — all 67 of them. That is a lot, so do a few words each day and stop while it is still fun. Take your time — there's no rush. Press your first word now, and tell me which one you chose!

overview.label: Overview
overview.text: Welcome! This page is our unit map. It shows what we will learn in Unit 1, "Welcome to School". We do this first so you know where we are going, like looking at a map before a trip. By the end you will know the five things this unit teaches, and you will have said your first English sentence out loud today. You need only your voice and your eyes. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are four small steps. Here comes step one. Step one: look at the picture at the top of the page. Tell me one thing you can see in it. One word is perfect — like "chair" or "book".

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the video lesson in Unit 1, Welcome to School. 🎒

This video is where we meet our new words: things in the classroom, colours, and how to say your own name. We do it by listening first, then saying the words out loud with our own voice. By the end you will be able to point to a table, a chair and a book, and say "My name is..." all by yourself. You need your ears, your voice, and one pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are five steps. Here is step one. Step one: get ready. Sit comfy, and put your pencil and paper next to you. Then say "Hello, school!" out loud in a big happy voice. I am listening — tell me when you have said it! 😊

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text: Today we are going to read a story together. It is called "Amal's First Day", and it is about a girl starting school for the very first time. We read it so you can hear lots of school words — like teacher, book, crayon and friend — inside a real story. By the end, you will be able to tell me what happened to Amal, and say some of the words yourself. You need your ears, your voice, and the story on your page. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are five steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Look at the picture and the title on your page. Do not read yet. Just look, and tell me one thing you think will happen in this story. A good answer is any guess in a few words, like "she meets a teacher" or "she is scared". There is no wrong guess here!

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher for this activity. 😊

This page is Comprehension. That means we listen to a story and then talk about it. Our story is "Amal's First Day". We do this so you can remember what happens and say it in English. Here is what I expect from you. Listen or read carefully, then answer with a word or a short sentence. Wrong answers are fine — trying is what helps you learn! There are six story questions. We will do one at a time. Step 1: Think about Amal's first day at school. In the story, a boy smiles at Amal and says hello. What is that boy's name?

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Grammar page. 😊

Grammar means the way we build a sentence so it sounds right in English. On this page we learn six little sentence patterns, like "This is a ___" and "I can ___". By the end, you will be able to say full sentences about your classroom, your name, your age and what you like. You need your voice, your eyes to look around the room, and one hand for pointing. That is all! Here is what I expect from you: say each sentence out loud, all the words, not just one word. Wobbly try is fine. Brave is better than perfect. There are six steps, one for each pattern. Here comes step one. Pattern 1 is: This is a ___. We say "a" before most words: a book, a pencil, a chair. But if the word starts with an open-mouth sound — a, e, i, o, u — we say "an": an apple, an egg. Now you try. Look around you, point to one thing, and type your sentence starting with "This is a".

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this is our Speaking page. 🙂

Speaking means we say the words out loud with our voice. We do it because English lives in your mouth, not just on the page — the more you say a word, the easier it becomes. By the end you will be able to point at school things and say "This is a ___." out loud, all by yourself. You need two things: your voice, and one real thing near you from school or home — a pencil, a book, or a chair is perfect. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look around you. Find one thing you can see right now. Just tell me what it is — one word is fine, like "pencil" or "book" or "chair".

writing.label: Writing
writing.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Writing page. We are starting with Writing 1, called "Draw and tell". You will draw your classroom, and then say and write one little sentence about it: This is a ___. We do this because drawing helps you find your idea first, and then the words come easily. By the end, you will have your very own picture with a real English sentence! Here is what I expect from you: a picture I can look at and know what it is, and your sentence starting with the words This is a. Wobbly letters are fine — brave tries are what count. There are four steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Get your things ready. You need paper, a pencil, and some crayons or colours. Ask your grown-up to help you find them if you need to. Tell me when you have them! 😊

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text:
Hello! Today we finish Unit 1 with our Welcome to School checkpoint. 🌟

It is a little quiz with ten questions. Each one gives you some words to choose from, and you pick the best one. We do it to show what you have learned about classroom things, colours, and saying your name and age. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, pick your own answer, and press the button on the page. I will help you think — but the answers must come from you. That way the quiz shows YOUR clever work. You will need your eyes, your ears, and a grown-up nearby to read with you. There are three steps before you begin. Here is step one. Step one: get ready. Sit comfortably, and ask your grown-up to read each question out loud with you. Tell me when you are ready. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are going to play the Classroom Treasure Hunt. 🎒

It is a looking game. I say a word, and you find that thing near you and say its name in English. We play it so the school words and colour words jump into your mouth quickly — table, chair, book, red, blue. What I expect from you: look with your eyes, then say a whole little sentence, like "I can see a red book." Loud and brave is best! A grown-up can play with you if one is nearby. There are 5 rounds. Here comes round one. Round 1: Find something BLUE. Point to it, then tell me: "I can see a blue ___."

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Activity 1: Colour and Say. 🎨

You will colour four things in the classroom picture. Then you will say each colour out loud. We do this so colour words like red and blue stay in your head, and so your mouth gets brave saying them. Here is what I expect from you. Neat colouring is nice, but it is not the important part. Scribbly is fine! The important part is the right colour on the right thing, and saying the colour word out loud. Get your crayons or colouring pencils ready, and your activity picture. There are four steps, one for each thing. Step 1: Find the book in the picture. Colour it red. As you colour, say out loud: "The book is red."

Tell me when you have done it. 😊

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text: Welcome to story time! Today we read the story on your Books page. It is called "Amal's First Day". We read it to meet Amal, who is starting school just like you. It gives us lots of school words, like teacher, chair, book and crayon. By the end, you will be able to tell me what happens in the story and say some school words out loud. You need three things: your book page, your pointing finger, and your voice. A grown-up can read with you, or you can press play and listen. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the title, "Amal's First Day", and the picture. Do not read yet. Just look and think. What I expect: tell me one thing you think will happen in the story. Any good guess counts — there is no wrong guess here! What do you think happens first? 😊

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Unit 2 start: Family Time. In this unit we learn the words for the people in your family, some breakfast foods, and how to count from one to ten. We do this so you can talk about your own family in English, out loud and with a big smile. By the end, you will be able to point at someone and say "This is my mum."

I expect you to say the words out loud with me, not just read them. Loud, brave voices, please! Spelling does not matter today — talking does. You need your voice, and a family photo or a piece of paper to draw on if you have one. A grown-up can sit with you too. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: say hello to me and tell me one person who lives in your family. Just one word is perfect, like "mum" or "brother".

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Let's start our video lesson for Unit 2, Family Time. 😊

In this lesson we meet the words for the people in our family, like mum, dad, sister, brother, grandma and grandpa. We also count from one to ten. We do this so you can talk about YOUR family in English, out loud and with confidence. By the end you will be able to point and say, "This is my mum."

You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. A family photo or a drawing helps too. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: hold up both hands and count with me, out loud: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. I expect to hear all ten numbers, said slowly and clearly, one number for each finger. Tell me when you have done it!

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text:
Lovely — let's do our story time together. 📖

Today's story is called "Breakfast at Grandma's House". It is about a girl named Amal who visits her grandma and grandpa. We read it to meet our new family words, and to practise counting. By the end, you will be able to tell me who is in Amal's family and what they eat. What you need: your ears, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. Here is what I expect from you: listen carefully, say some words out loud with me, and try to answer even if you are not sure. Trying is the important part. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the title, "Breakfast at Grandma's House". Before we read, tell me one thing you think will happen in this story. There is no wrong answer!

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Vocabulary page of Unit 2, Family Time. Vocabulary means the new words we learn. In this unit the words are about your family, breakfast food, and numbers one to ten. By the end you will be able to say who is in your family and talk about them out loud in English. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, not just in your head, and then make your own sentence with it. Talking is the real work today. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. We will do this in four steps. Let's start with something small. Step one: three family words. mum — the woman who looks after you at home. My mum makes warm bread. dad — the man who looks after you at home. My dad tells funny stories. grandma — the mother of your mum or your dad. Grandma tells us lovely stories. Say all three out loud, slowly. Then tell me: which one of these three people did you see today? 😊

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Family Time talking practice. 😊

On this page we learn six special sentence patterns. A pattern is like a little box, and you put your own words inside it. We do this so you can talk about your family in English, out loud and with confidence. By the end, you will be able to say who is in your family, ask a question, and tell me how you help at home. You need your voice, and a family photo or a drawing if you have one nearby. A grown-up can sit with you too. There are six steps, one for each pattern. Here comes step one. Pattern one is: This is my ___. Say it out loud, and put a family word in the space. Like: This is my mum. I would love three sentences from you, with three different people. Say the little word "is" clearly in the middle. Type your three sentences here when you are ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Welcome to our Speaking lesson! Today you will talk about your family out loud. We do this because speaking is the best way to make new words stick. By the end, you will be able to say "This is my mum" and more, all by yourself. What I expect: you say the words out loud in a clear voice, not just in your head. Brave voice, even if it is not perfect! You need a family photo or a drawing of your family. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are six speaking steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Look at your family picture. Point to one person and say out loud: "This is my mum." Then point to another and say "This is my dad."

When you have said both, type "done" and tell me who you pointed to. 😊

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Comprehension page. 📖

Comprehension means showing that you understood the story. Our story is "Breakfast at Grandma's House". We do this so you can listen well, remember, and answer in your own words. Here is what I expect from you: answer out loud in a full try, even a short one. Two or three words is fine. If you are not sure, say "I'm stuck" and I will give you a hint, not the answer. We have three steps: first we read, then six story questions, then some talking lines. Step 1: Read the story on your page, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. You can also press the listen button and hear it. As you read, look out for the people in Amal's family. Tell me when you have finished, and we will start question one.

writing.label: Writing
writing.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Writing 1, called "Draw and tell." 🎨

You will draw your family sitting together at dinner, count the people, and then say who they are using our sentence: "This is my ___."

We do this because drawing helps you think first, and talking helps the words stick. By the end you will be able to point at your family and say their names in English. You need paper, a pencil and some crayons. There are five little steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Get your paper, pencil and crayons ready. Tell me when you have them!

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Let's start Activity 1. It is called Point and Say. In this activity you point at the people in your family picture and name them out loud. We do it so your mouth gets used to the English words for family. By the end, you will be able to say "This is my mother" all by yourself. You need your family drawing or a family photo, and your speaking voice. 😊

Here is what I expect: four people pointed at, and the whole sentence said out loud each time — "This is my ___" — not just one word. There are five little steps. Here comes step one. Get your family drawing or a family photo and put it in front of you. If you don't have one, draw four people quickly — that is fine! Tell me when it is ready.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are playing the Family Time games. 🎲

Games are how we practise talking. When we play, the words come out easily, and English starts to feel like fun, not work. By the end you will be able to count to ten, ask "Do you like...?", and say who is in your family — out loud and with a big voice. You need just three things: your voice, your ten fingers, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. There are three little games. Here comes game one! Game 1: Ten Fingers. Hold up all ten fingers. Count them out loud, slowly: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. I expect you to say every number out loud, and touch one finger for each number. No skipping! Type "done" when you have counted, and tell me the last number you said.

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text: Hello! Today we do the Family Time checkpoint. That is a little quiz about our unit. It has ten questions. Each one shows you some words, and you pick the one best answer. We do it to see what you already know about family words, like mum, dad, grandma and brother. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, think, then choose. And this is a test, so the answers must come from you. I will help you get ready, but I cannot tell you which one to click. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: get ready. Sit up nice and tall. Take one slow breath. Then tell me: are you ready to start?

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text: Today we are going to read a story together. It is called "Breakfast at Grandma's House". It is about a girl called Amal who visits her grandma and grandpa. We read stories so we can hear new words and say them out loud. By the end, you will be able to name the people in Amal's family and count some fruit with her. You need your listening ears, your talking voice, and the story on your page. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: look at the title, "Breakfast at Grandma's House". Do not read yet. Just tell me one thing you think will happen in this story. A good answer is one small idea, like "they eat food" or "she hugs grandma". Off you go!

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are starting Unit 3: Fun and Games. 🎈

This page is the Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It shows you what we will learn: action words like bounce and catch, the names of body parts, and words that tell where a ball is. We are doing this so you know what is coming, and so you feel ready. You need only two things: your body to move, and your voice to talk. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Stand up and do three actions with me. Jump one time. Clap your hands. Then pretend to catch a ball. I expect you to really move your body, and then tell me which one was the most fun. Off you go!

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Vocabulary page of Unit 3, Fun and Games. Vocabulary means the new words we learn. In this unit the words are about playing games, our body, and where things are. By the end you will be able to say the words and use them in your own sentence. You need your voice, your body to act the words, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are 4 steps. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, do the action with your body, then make your own little sentence. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Our first word is bounce. Bounce means to make a ball jump up again after it hits the ground. Like this: I bounce the ball outside. Now you try. Say "bounce" out loud, and pretend to bounce a ball with your hand. Then tell me: did you do it? 🏀

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the video lesson. This lesson is called Fun and Games. We watch, we listen, and we move our bodies with the words. We do it because play helps words stick. By the end, you will say game words like bounce, roll, throw and catch, and touch and name parts of your body. You need three things: your voice, a little space to move, and a ball or a soft toy. No ball? A rolled-up sock works too! There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: press play on the video, stand up, and copy every action you see. I expect you to move your body, not just watch. Try to say the words out loud with the video, even if they feel wobbly. Tell me when you have done step one. Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Comprehension. 📚

Comprehension means listening to a story and then talking about it. We do it so you can remember the story and say what happened in your own words. Our story is "Amal and the Big Ball."

You need your ears, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are six questions. I will give you one at a time, and you tell me your answer. Here comes question one. In the story, Amal has a big ball. What colour is her ball?

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text: Today we are going to read a story together. It is called "Amal and the Big Ball". It is about three friends, a red ball, and a ball that gets stuck in a tree! We read stories to hear new words and to talk about how people feel. By the end, you will be able to tell me what happened in the story and use our new words like bounce, roll, throw and catch. Here is what I expect from you: listen or read carefully, say the action words out loud with me, and try to answer my questions in a full sentence. Guessing is allowed! Mistakes are how we learn. You need the story on your page, your voice, and a little space to move your arms. There are 5 steps. Step 1. Look at the title: "Amal and the Big Ball". What do you think happens in this story? Tell me one guess. 🙂

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Grammar page. 🎈

Grammar means the way we build our sentences. On this page we learn six talking patterns for games and play. By the end, you will be able to say a whole sentence and do the action with your body. You need your voice, a little space to move, and a ball or a soft toy if you have one. A grown-up can sit with you. Here comes step one of six. Our first pattern is: I can ___. Pick one thing you are good at, like hop, catch or climb. Say the WHOLE sentence out loud, and do the action while you say it. I expect a full sentence, not just one word. So "I can hop." — not only "hop."

Now you try one, and I'll watch. Tell me your sentence!

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Speaking. Speaking means we use our voice out loud. In this activity you will say fun game words like run, jump and catch. We do it so English feels easy in your mouth, not just in your eyes. By the end, you will be able to say "I can ___" all by yourself. You need only two things: your voice, and a little space to move. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Listen and copy me. I say: "I can run." Now you stand up, run on the spot, and say it out loud: "I can run."

I expect a whole sentence, not just the word run. Type "done" when you have said it. 🙂

writing.label: Writing
writing.text:
Hello! Today I am your writing teacher. 📝

On this page we do our Fun and Games writing. You will draw, trace, and write tiny sentences about playing. By the end you will be able to write a sentence like "I can throw." That is real writing, all by you! You need paper, a pencil, and crayons. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. We will start with Writing 1: Draw and tell. It has three small steps. Step 1: Think of your favourite game. Ball games, running games, hide and seek — any game you love. Tell me now: what game do you like to play best?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Activity 1. 🙂

This activity is called "Point and say". You will look at four toys in your picture: a ball, a kite, blocks, and a skipping rope. You will point to each one and say a sentence out loud. We do this so your mouth gets used to saying English toy words. By the end, you will be able to name four toys and say a whole sentence about them. You need your Activities page open, your finger for pointing, and your voice. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Look at the picture and find the ball. Point to it with your finger. Then say out loud: "I like to play with the ball."

I want to hear a whole sentence, not just the word "ball". Say it nice and clear. Tell me when you have done it!

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Books page. 📚

Here we read our unit story, "Amal and the Big Ball". We read it to meet our new play words like bounce, roll, throw and catch. By the end, you will be able to tell me what happened in the story and act out the words with your body. You need your ears, your voice, and a little space to move. A grown-up can read the story with you if one is nearby. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: look at the story title, "Amal and the Big Ball". Do not read yet — just think. What do you think happens in this story? I expect one guess, in a few words. Any guess is a good guess!

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are going to play the games in Unit 3, Fun and Games. 🎈

Games are how we learn English in this unit. When your body moves, your mouth remembers the word! By the end you will be able to say and do action words like jump and clap, touch and name parts of your body, and say where a ball is — on, under or next to something. You will need: space to stand up, and a ball or a soft toy or even a rolled-up sock. A grown-up nearby can play with you if one is there. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: stand up and get ready. Find a safe space where you can jump without bumping anything, and put your ball or soft toy next to you. I expect you to be standing, with your ball ready, and to tell me "ready" when you are. Take your time — there's no rush.

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the Fun and Games checkpoint — that is your quiz. 🙂

It has ten little questions about the words we played with: action words like jump and bounce, body parts like nose, and where things are, like on and under. We do it so you can show what your brain has learned. You do not need a pencil — just your eyes, your ears, and a grown-up nearby to read the words with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, choose only one answer, and try your very best. I really can't give quiz answers — but I promise you can get this. I can give you hints and warm-up practice. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Get ready. Sit somewhere comfy. If a grown-up is near, ask them to sit with you and read the words out loud. Then tell me "ready".

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are starting Unit 4: Making Things. This page is the Overview. It is like a map of everything we will learn. We look at the map first so you know where we are going. By the end of this page, you will be able to say what this unit is about and say one making sentence out loud. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you have one nearby. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Say the unit name out loud, twice: "Making Things."

Then tell me one thing you think we will make. A hat? A card? A picture? Any guess is a good guess.

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text: Hello! Today we are learning the new words for Unit 4, Making Things. This is our Vocabulary activity. We learn the words first, so that later you can talk about the shapes and colours you make. By the end, you will be able to name shapes and say them in your own sentence. You just need your voice, and a pencil if you like. There are three steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Let's learn three new words together. A square has four straight sides, all the same size. Think of a window. A circle is round with no corners. Think of the sun. A triangle has three straight sides and three pointy corners. Think of a slice of pizza. Now say them out loud with me, slowly: square... circle... triangle. When you have said all three, tell me "done" and we will go on. 😊

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the video lesson of Unit 4, Making Things. 🎨

This lesson is our warm-up for the whole unit. We will learn shape words, colour words, and the talk lines we use when we make things. By the end you will be able to point at something and say, "This is a circle," and "I am making a hat."

You need three things: your eyes to look, your voice to say the words out loud, and something round nearby, like a cup or a plate. We have four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: shapes. Look around your room and find something round with no corners. A plate, a cup, a coin, a clock. Point at it and say out loud: "This is a circle."

What round thing did you find?

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Comprehension page. 📚

Comprehension means "understanding the story". We listened to the story Amal Makes a Mat. Now I will ask you some questions about it, and you tell me what you remember. Why do we do this? Because a good reader does not just hear words — a good reader thinks about them. By the end, you will be able to tell me what happened in the story and how the people felt. What I expect from you: just say your answer out loud or type it. Short answers are perfect. If you are not sure, guess — mistakes are how we learn. You need the story on your page, and your thinking brain. There are six questions about Amal's story. Here comes question one. What are Amal and Ayeeyo making under the big tree?

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Grammar page of Making Things. 📦

Grammar means the small words that make a sentence sound right — like "a" and "an" and "am". We do this so you can talk about the things you make and wear, all by yourself. There are six little steps, one for each sentence pattern. In each step I will say a pattern, and I expect you to make ONE sentence of your own with it, and type it to me. Say it out loud first, then type it. You need nothing but your voice and your eyes — just look around the room! Here comes step one. Our pattern is: This is a ___. Look around you and find one thing you could make something with — paper, a box, a straw, a cup. Now tell me: This is a ___.

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text:
Hello! Today we are reading the story on your page, "Amal Makes a Mat". 📖

We read it to meet our new unit words, like circle, square, triangle and rectangle, and to find out what Amal makes with her grandmother. By the end you will be able to tell me what happens in the story and say some shape and colour words out loud. What I expect from you: listen or read carefully, say the words out loud with me, and try an answer even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 5 steps. Here is step one. Step 1: Get ready. Sit comfy, find the story on your page, and press play or start reading the first part. Read up to where Amal says, "I want to make a mat too!"

Tell me when you have done that.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! Today we are doing our Speaking practice for Making Things. 🎨

Speaking means we say the words out loud. We do it so your mouth gets strong and brave with English words. By the end, you will be able to name shapes, colours and clothes, and say what you are making. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. Paper and crayons help too! There are six small speaking steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Say the shape names out loud. Say these three, nice and clear:
This is a circle. This is a square. This is a triangle. I expect a whole sentence each time, not just one word. Say them out loud now, then type "done" and tell me which one felt hardest to say.

writing.label: Writing
writing.text:
Hello! Today I am your writing teacher, and we are doing Writing 1: Draw and Tell. In this activity you draw something you have made, then say and write a little about it. We do this because good writing starts with a good idea — first we say it, then we write it. By the end you will have a drawing and one small sentence: "This is a ___."

You will need paper, a pencil and some crayons. There are four small steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Think of something you have made from paper or blocks. A hat, a card, a tower, a boat — anything real that you made. Tell me what it is!

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Activity 1: Colour and Say. You will colour four shapes and say the name of each one out loud. We do this so your eyes learn the shapes and your mouth learns the words at the same time. By the end, you will be able to point at a shape and say "This is a circle" all by yourself. You need your activity page, four crayons (red, blue, green and yellow), and your voice. There are four steps — one shape each time. Here comes step one! Find the circle. A circle is round with no corners. Colour it red, and while you colour, say out loud: "This is a red circle."

I am listening for a clear "circle" and nice bright colouring. Going outside the lines is perfectly fine! 🙂

Tell me when you have done it.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Making Things games. Games are how we practise our shape words, colour words and dressing-up words while we have fun. By the end, you will be able to name shapes, say a colour and a shape together, and say who you can pretend to be. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby to listen. There are four games. Here comes game one — the Shape Riddle. I say the clue, you say the shape. I am round. I have no corners. I look like the sun. What shape am I? 🙂

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Making Things checkpoint. 🌟

This is a little quiz with ten questions. It shows what you learned about shapes, colours, clothes and making things. You just choose the best word or sentence from the choices on your screen. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, think carefully, then pick your own answer. I will not tell you the answers — but I will help you know HOW to choose, and I will cheer you on. Have a grown-up nearby if you need help reading. There are three steps: first we warm up, then you do the questions, then we look back at what you learned. Step 1 — the warm-up. Let me show you a similar example first. If I asked: "Which word names a colour? tree, blue, jump" — the answer is blue, because blue is a colour we can see. Tree is a thing and jump is an action. Now you try one like it, just for practice: which word names a shape — hat, square, or cut?

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text:
Welcome to our story time! On this page we have our unit story, "Amal Makes a Mat". We read it because stories give us new words like weave, bumpy and patient — and this one teaches us something lovely: good things take time. Here is what I expect from you today. Listen or read carefully, join in with the parts that repeat, and tell me what you think in your own words. Even one or two words is a great answer. You need the story on your screen, and your voice. A grown-up can read it with you if one is nearby. We have four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: read or listen to the first part of the story, up to where Amal says "Oh no! My mat is not good."

While you read, look for the words Amal and Ayeeyo. Ayeeyo means grandmother. Tell me when you have done that part. 🌿

overview.label: Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 5, On the Farm! This first page is our tour of the unit. We look at what we will learn, so your brain knows what is coming — just like looking at a map before a trip. By the end of this unit you will name farm animals, make their sounds, name farm things like barn and tractor, and say what animals are doing. Today all you need is your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Tell me what you already know about farms. Say or type one thing you think lives on a farm. Even one word is a great answer — like "cow" or "eggs".

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text:
Hello! Today we are learning the farm words in Unit 5. Vocabulary means the new words we know and can say. We are doing this so you can talk about a farm in English — the animals, the sounds they make, and the things you see there. You only need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are four steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Let's learn three animal words together. cow — a big animal that gives us milk
hen — a bird that lays eggs
chick — a baby bird, just out of its egg

Say each word out loud, slowly. Then tell me: which one is the baby? 🐣

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the video lesson for Unit 5: On the Farm. 🐄

This is our first look at the farm. You will watch and listen, and you will say words out loud with me. By the end you will be able to name farm animals, make their sounds, and say what they are doing. What I expect from you: a loud, happy voice. You do not need to write anything. Just look, listen, and say the words after me. It is fine to get things wrong — that is how we learn. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Warm up. Think about a farm. Tell me one animal you think lives there. Just one word is enough!

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text: Welcome to our story lesson! Today we are reading "Amal and the Little Hen". It is about a girl who helps her grandmother on a farm. We read this story to meet our farm words — cow, hen, barn, seed, egg — and to hear how a story goes from beginning to end. By the end, you will be able to tell me what happened in the story, and make the animal sounds out loud. What you need: the story on your screen, your voice, and your listening ears. A grown-up can read with you if one is nearby. Here is what I expect from you: read or listen carefully, say the words out loud with me, and try an answer even if you are not sure. Trying is the best part. There are 5 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Look at the picture and the title, "Amal and the Little Hen". Do not read yet. Just guess. What do you think happens in this story? Tell me one idea.

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text: Hello! Today we are doing Comprehension. That means we listen to a story, then answer questions about it. Our story is "Amal and the Little Hen" — a girl who helps on her grandmother's farm. We do this so you can remember a story and talk about it out loud. That is a big reading skill! Here is what I expect from you: say your answers out loud, in your own words. Short answers are fine. You can point at the page too. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 6 questions. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. In the story, Amal and Ayeeyo go to see the animals. Which animal did they see first?

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Grammar page for On the Farm. 🐄

Grammar here means the little sentence patterns we use to talk about the farm. We practise them out loud so speaking English feels easy and happy. By the end you will be able to say six farm sentences all by yourself. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if there is one. That's all! There are six patterns, and we will do one at a time. Here comes step one. Pattern 1 is: This is a ___. We use it to point at an animal and name it. Like this: This is a cow. There is one small trick. Before words like ox and egg, we say "an" instead of "a", because they start with an open-mouth sound. So we say: This is an ox. Now you try one. Pick a farm animal and say the whole sentence to me.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! Today we are doing our Speaking activities for "On the Farm."

Speaking means you use your voice out loud. We are doing this so you can say farm words clearly and feel brave when you talk in English. By the end, you will be able to name farm animals, make their sounds, and say what they are doing. You need just two things: your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. 😊

There are six little speaking turns. We will do one at a time. Step 1 — Listen and point. Say these three sentences out loud, nice and clear:
This is a cow. This is a hen. This is a sheep. I want to hear whole sentences, not just one word. Say each one slowly. Type "done" when you have said all three, or type them here to me.

writing.label: Writing
writing.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Writing page. 📝

This is Writing 1, called "Draw and tell". You will draw a little farm, then write one small sentence about it. We do this because drawing helps us find the words first — and then writing is easy. By the end you will have your own farm picture with a real English sentence on it. You need paper and a pencil, and some crayons if you have them. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Draw a farm. Put two animals in it, and one plant that is growing. Any animals you like — a cow, a hen, a duck, a goat. I am looking for two animals and one plant. They do not have to be neat. Big and bright is best! Tell me when your drawing is done.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are starting the Activities page for our farm unit. 🐮

First we will do Activity 1. You colour four farm animals — a pig, a cow, a chick and a duck — and you say each animal's name out loud. We do this because saying the words while you colour helps you remember them. By the end you will be able to point to four farm animals and name them all by yourself. You need your crayons: pink, brown and yellow. There are four little steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Find the pig on your page. Colour it pink. As you colour, say out loud: "This is a pig."

I am listening for a nice clear "pig". Any shade of pink is fine — neat colouring is not the important part, the word is! Tell me when you have done it. Take your time — there's no rush.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are playing the farm games in Unit 5, On the Farm. Games are how we make the farm words stick — we colour, we make animal sounds, we move like the animals, and we say the words out loud. By the end you will be able to name farm animals, say the sound each one makes, and point out farm things like the barn and the tractor. You will need crayons, a piece of paper, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. Here is what I expect from you: try every game, say the words OUT LOUD (not just in your head), and tell me when each one is done. Mistakes are how we learn. There are three games today. Let's start with something small. Game 1: Colour the farm animals. Draw or colour four animals — the pig pink, the cow brown, the chick yellow, and the duck white. The duck can stay white, that is fine! As you colour each one, point at it and say its name out loud: "This is a pig."

A good job looks like this: four animals coloured, and four names said out loud. Off you go — tell me when you are done. 🎨

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text:
Hello! Today you are doing the On the Farm checkpoint. It is a little quiz with ten questions about farm animals, their sounds, and farm words. We do it to show what you can already do — it is not scary, it is a chance to shine. You just need your eyes, your ears, and your brave voice. One thing first: I cannot tell you the answers, but I will help you think. 🐮

There are three steps before the quiz, then you will do the questions. Step 1: Warm up your farm words. Say these out loud right now: cow, hen, duck, sheep, goat. Then make three sounds: moo, cluck, baa. Tell me when you have said them all!

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text:
Hello! Today we are reading our farm story, "Amal and the Little Hen". 📖

This is our Books activity. We read a story together so we can hear the new farm words in a real story, and so you can join in with the animal sounds. By the end you will know what happens to Amal, and you will be able to say some farm words out loud all by yourself. You need three things: the story on your page, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are five steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Look at the title, "Amal and the Little Hen". Do not read yet — just guess! What do you think happens in this story? Any guess is a good guess. Tell me your idea.

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today we start Unit 6: My Five Senses. This page is our map. It shows what we will learn: our five senses, the body parts we use, and fun words like soft, loud and sweet. We do this so you can talk about the world around you in English. By the end of today's little tour, you will be able to name all five senses and point to the body part for each one. You need only two things: your body, and your voice. That's it! There are 4 short steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Touch your eyes gently with your fingers. Then say out loud: "I can see with my eyes."

I expect one clear sentence, said out loud, with the word "eyes" at the end. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have said it!

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text:
Hello! Today we are learning the words for our five senses. Your senses are the five ways your body learns about the world. We learn these words so you can talk about everything you see, hear, smell, taste and touch. By the end, you will be able to say each word and use it in your own sentence. You need just two things: your voice, and your body! No pencil yet. We will do three words, one at a time. Here comes the first one. Step 1. The word is see. See means to use your eyes to look at something. Point to your eyes with two fingers. Then say: "I can see with my eyes."

Now tell me one thing you can see right now. 👀

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our video lesson for Unit 6: My Five Senses. In this lesson you will watch and listen, and I will help you join in. We do this so the words go into your eyes AND your ears AND your hands — that is how they stick! By the end, you will be able to name your five senses and say "I can see with my eyes."

You need three things: the video on your screen, your voice, and your own body. Your eyes, ears, nose, tongue and hands are your tools today! A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Sit up nice and tall. Now press play on the video and watch the first part. Listen carefully for the word "senses". When you hear it, wave your hand in the air! Tell me when you have done that. 👋

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the story part of Unit 6. Our story is called "Amal at the Market". It is about a girl who goes to a busy market with her grandmother and uses all five of her senses. We read stories like this so you can hear new words in a real story, not just on a word list. By the end, you will be able to tell me what Amal saw, heard, smelled, tasted and touched. What I expect from you: listen or read carefully, say the words out loud with me, and answer my little questions in your own words. Short answers are perfect. Just try — that is all I ask. You need the story on your screen, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Hold up one hand. Count your five senses on your five fingers with me: see, hear, smell, taste, touch. Now tell me which body part you use to SEE.

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Comprehension. That means I ask you questions about our story, "Amal at the Market", and you tell me the answers. We do this so you can listen carefully, remember what happened, and say your answer in a full sentence. By the end, you will be able to talk about the story and about the five senses. You just need your ears, your voice, and the story on your page. 😊

Here is what I expect from you: answer out loud or type it, use your own words, and try to say a whole sentence, not just one word. Take your time — there's no rush. There are six story questions. Here comes question one. In the story, Amal goes to a big, busy market. But she does not go alone. Someone took her there. Who took Amal to the busy market?

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Grammar page. 🌟

This page is called Language Practice. We learn six little sentence patterns about our five senses — like "I can see with my eyes." We practise saying them out loud, because speaking comes first, then writing. By the end, you will be able to say all five senses, describe how things feel, and compare two things. You need three things: your voice, your body (eyes, ears, nose, hands!), and one grown-up nearby if you have one. Here is what I expect from you: say each sentence out loud in a big clear voice, then type it to me. Full sentence, not just one word. Take your time — there's no rush. There are six steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Eyes are for seeing. Cover your eyes with your hands. Now open them wide and say: "I can see with my eyes."

Then look around you and find three things you can see. Type your sentence and your three things to me.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! Today I am your speaking teacher. 😊

This activity is called Listen and Point. You will hear a body part, point to it on your own face, and then say a whole sentence out loud. We do this because saying words out loud helps them stick in your mouth and your memory. By the end, you will be able to say "I can see with my eyes" all by yourself, in a clear voice. You need just two things: your voice, and your hands ready to point. A grown-up nearby can listen to you too. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Point to your eyes with one finger. Then say out loud, nice and slow: "I can see with my eyes."

I expect a clear voice and the word "eyes" with a buzzy z sound at the end — eyezzz. Tell me when you have said it!

writing.label: Writing
writing.text: Welcome to Writing time! Today we do Writing 1 — Draw and Tell. You will draw your own face, then say and write what your eyes can do. We do this so you can name your senses and write one good sentence about them. By the end you will have a face drawing and the sentence: I can see with my eyes. You need paper, a pencil, and your voice. There are 4 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Draw a big circle for your face. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when your circle is done. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we will do Activity 1 together. In this activity you draw a line from each body part to its job. Eyes, ears, nose and tongue each have a job to do. We do this so you can say which sense goes with which part of your body. By the end, you will be able to say, "I can see with my eyes."

You need your activity page and a pencil. You also need your voice, because we will say the words out loud too! There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: touch each body part on your face and name it. Touch your eyes and say "eyes". Then your ears, your nose, and your tongue. I expect you to name all four, out loud, in a clear voice. Tell me when you have done it. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are going to play the Senses Game. In this game, I say something you can see, hear, smell, taste or touch. You tell me which sense you use, and which body part does the job. We play it because it helps you say sentences like "I hear with my ears" all by yourself. You need just two things: your voice, and your body! You can point to your eyes, ears, nose, tongue and hands as you play. There are 4 steps in our game. Here is step one. Step 1: Warm up your body parts. Point to each one and say it out loud: "These are my eyes. These are my ears. This is my nose. This is my tongue. These are my hands."

I expect you to say all five out loud, and touch each part as you say it. Tell me when you have done it! 😊

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text: Hello! Today you are doing the My Five Senses checkpoint. That is a little quiz with ten questions about our senses. We do it to see what your brain has already learned — seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. By the end, you will know which parts you are strong at. Here is what I expect from you. Read each question twice. Choose the answer you think is best, all by yourself. I will not give you the answers, but I promise you can get this. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: get ready. Point to your eyes, your ears, your nose, your tongue and your hands. Say each one out loud as you point. Tell me when you have done it.

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text:
Today we are reading our unit story, "Amal at the Market". It is about a little girl who goes to a busy market with her grandmother and uses all five senses. We read stories like this to meet our new words in a real story, and to hear how people talk about what they see, hear, smell, taste and touch. By the end, you will be able to tell me what Amal did with each sense, and say your own sentence like "I can see with my eyes."

What you need: your eyes on the story page, and your voice ready to talk to me. You can point to your body parts too! What I expect from you: try to read or listen carefully, and answer me in your own words. You do not have to be perfect. Trying is what counts. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Look at the title, "Amal at the Market". Do not read the story yet. Just think and tell me: what do you think Amal will see at a market?

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today we start Unit 7. It is called "Let's Go!" 🚌

This is our video lesson. We watch and listen, and we join in. It is all about how we travel — walking, buses, cars, bicycles and boats. By the end you will be able to say how YOU get to school. Here is what I expect from you: sit up, say the words out loud with me, and do the actions with your hands. Talking is more important than writing today! There are four steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Before we watch, tell me one way people travel. Just one word is perfect. What do you say?

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today we start Unit 7. It is called "Let's Go!"

This unit is all about how we travel — walking, buses, cars, bicycles and boats. We do it so you can tell anyone, in English, how you get to school and where you go. By the end you will say things like "I go by bus" all by yourself. You need only two things: your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. Speaking out loud is the work here — spelling can wait. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step one: think about your morning. How do you get to school? Say it out loud first, then type it here in any words you like. Even one word is a good answer.

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text: Hello! Today we are going to read a story together. It is called "Amal's Big Bus Ride". We read it to hear travel words like walk, bus, seat and boat in a real story. By the end, you will be able to tell me how Amal got to Grandmother's house. Here is what I expect from you: read or listen to each part, then answer my one question in your own words. Speaking your answer out loud is perfect — you do not need to write. You need the story on your page, and your voice. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Look at the title, "Amal's Big Bus Ride". Do not read yet! Just tell me — what do you think will happen in this story?

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text:
Welcome to our Vocabulary lesson, Unit 7: Let's Go! 🚌

This page teaches the words for how we travel. We learn them because then you can tell anyone how YOU get to school — in English! By the end, you will be able to say three travel words and use each one in your own sentence. You need only your voice and your brain. A grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. We have 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: the word BUS. A bus is a long vehicle that carries many people at once. Like the yellow bus that takes children to school. Say it with me, slowly: bus. Now make your own sentence with it. Tell me your sentence, and I will read it.

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Comprehension page. 📚

Comprehension means showing that you understood the story. Our story is "Amal's Big Bus Ride". I will ask you questions about it, and you will answer out loud or type them to me. Why do we do this? Because good readers remember what happens and can talk about it. By the end, you will be able to tell me about Amal's journey in your own words. What I expect from you: try every question, even if you are not sure. A guess is always better than nothing. Short answers are fine — one or two words is enough for many of them. You will need the story on your page. There are 6 story questions. Step 1. Before we answer anything, let's read it together. Read the story on your page, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Look at the pictures too. Tell me "done" when you have read it. Take your time — there's no rush.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text: Hello! Today we are doing Speaking 1: Listen and point. This activity is all about saying how you travel. We do it so you can tell anyone, in English, how you get to school. By the end, you will say three travel sentences out loud, nice and clear. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if there is one. There are 3 little steps. Step 1: Say these words after me, out loud, one at a time. bus... car... foot. I expect you to say each word clearly, not in your head — out loud! Tell me when you have said all three. 🚌Hello! Today we are doing Speaking 1: Listen and point. This activity is all about saying how you travel. We do it so you can tell anyone, in English, how you get to school. By the end, you will say three travel sentences out loud, nice and clear. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if there is one. There are 3 little steps. Step 1: Say these words after me, out loud, one at a time. bus... car... foot. I expect you to say each word clearly, not in your head — out loud! Tell me when you have said all three. 🚌

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today I am your English teacher, and this is our Talking Sentences activity. 🚌

On this page we learn six special sentence patterns about travel. A pattern is a sentence with a gap, like "I go by ___." We fill the gap with our own word. Why? So you can tell anyone in English how you travel. By the end, you will say six travel sentences all by yourself. What I expect from you: say each sentence out loud, in full — not just one word. You can do the action too! You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby is lovely. There are six steps, one for each pattern. Here comes step one. Pattern one is: I go by ___. Say it out loud three times, with a different way to travel each time. Like bus, car, or boat. Hold an imaginary steering wheel as you say it! Little tip: we say "I go by bus" — no "a" in the middle. Tell me your three sentences when you're ready.

writing.label: Writing
writing.text: Hello! Today I am your writing teacher, and we are doing Writing 1: Draw and tell. In this activity you draw your journey to school, then say and write how you travel. We do it because writing starts with a picture and a spoken idea. By the end, you will have your own picture with the words "I go by ___" and one safe thing you do on the way. You need paper, a pencil and some crayons. Get them ready! Here is what I expect from you: say your idea out loud first, then draw it, then try the words. Neat is nice, but brave trying is better. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: think and say. Tell me how you go to school. Say it out loud like this: I go by bus. Or I go by car. Or I walk. Now tell me — how do you go to school?

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are playing the Let's Go! games. 🚌

These games help you say the travel words out loud — bus, car, boat, bicycle — and tell how things move. By the end you will be able to name six ways to travel and say a whole sentence about them. You need your crayons or colouring pencils, some paper, and your voice. There are six little games, and we will do one at a time. Here is Game 1. Colour four vehicles on your page: the bus yellow, the car red, the boat blue, and the bicycle green. Then point to each one and say its name out loud. I am expecting four colours in the right places, and four words said clearly. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you are done!

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text: Welcome to our Books page! Today we read a story called "Amal's Big Bus Ride". It is about a girl who travels a long way to see her grandmother. We read it to learn travel words like walk, bus and boat, and to talk about the story. Here is what I expect from you: read or listen to each part, then tell me your answer in your own words. Your answer does not have to be perfect. Trying is the important part! There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Look at the story on your page. Read the title out loud: "Amal's Big Bus Ride". Then tell me one thing you think will happen in this story.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Activity 1. In this activity you colour four vehicles and say their names out loud. We do it because colours help us remember new words, and saying words out loud makes them stick. By the end, you will name a bus, a car, a boat and a bicycle all by yourself. You need crayons and your activity sheet. I expect you to say each word out loud, nice and clear — not just colour quietly. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Find the bus on your page. Point to it with your finger and say "bus" out loud. Then colour it yellow. Tell me when you have done it. 🚌

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text:
Hello! Today we do the Let's Go! checkpoint. It has ten little questions about travelling — buses, boats, planes and safe walking. You read each one and pick the best answer. It shows you how much you have learned in this unit. All you need is your eyes, your ears, and a grown-up beside you to read the words. 🚌

Here is what I expect from you: read the question twice, say your answer out loud, then click it. I can help you think — but the answers must come from you. That way the checkpoint shows YOUR clever brain. There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: a warm-up, not the quiz. Let's practise the thinking. I say a vehicle, and you tell me where it goes — land, water or sky. Ready? Where does a boat go?

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 8: Wonderful Water! 💧

This page is our map of the whole unit. We look at it first so you know what is coming, just like looking at a menu before you eat. By the end of this unit you will be able to say where water comes from, how we use it, and which animals live in water. You need only two things today: your voice, and your eyes on the screen. There are 4 short steps. Step 1: Look at the picture at the top of the page. Then tell me one thing you can see in it. Just one word is perfect — like "rain" or "water". I am waiting for your word! 😊

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the video lesson in Unit 8, Wonderful Water. 💧

In this lesson we meet water words and say them out loud. We do it so you can talk about water in English — where it comes from and how you use it. By the end you will say three water words clearly and one full sentence about water. You need: your voice, your ears, and if a grown-up is near, they can sit with you. A cup of water or a tap nearby is a lovely extra. There are 4 steps. Here is step one. Step 1: Get ready. Sit up nicely and take a big breath. Then say this word out loud, slowly, with me: water. I expect you to say it loud enough for someone in the room to hear. When you have said it, type "done" and tell me one place you can see water right now.

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text:
Hello! Today we are learning our water words for Unit 8, Wonderful Water. 💧

This activity is all about saying new words out loud and knowing what they mean. We do it so you can talk about water, rain and weather in English, all by yourself. By the end, you will be able to say some water words and use them in your own little sentence. You need your voice, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. That's all! We will do this in three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: our first three words are water, rain and drop. Water is the clear drink that fills rivers and cups. Rain is drops of water falling down from the clouds. A drop is one tiny bit of water, smaller than your fingertip. Say each word out loud, slowly. Then tell me: which one of the three do you like best?

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text:
Hello! Today I am your reading teacher. 📖

This activity is our story, "The Well in the Village". It is about a girl named Amal, a deep well, and rain that comes at last. We read stories like this so we hear new English words and understand what happens and why. By the end, you will be able to tell me the story in your own words and say two or three new water words. You need your eyes on the story page, your listening ears, and your voice. There are five steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the title, "The Well in the Village". Do not read yet — just guess. What do you think a well is, and what do you think this story will be about? A good answer is one or two sentences of your own guessing. There is no wrong guess here!

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Comprehension activity. Comprehension means showing that you understood the story. We just listened to "The Well in the Village" — a story about Amal, her brother Adam, and their village well. By the end you will be able to answer questions about the story out loud, in your own words. Here is what I expect from you: say your answer out loud first, then type it to me. A short answer is perfect. You do not need long sentences, and you do not need perfect spelling. Just tell me what you remember. There are two parts. Part one is six questions about the story. Part two is six talking lines. That is twelve small steps. Ready? Here comes question one. Who walked to the well with Amal every morning?

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text: Hello! Today we are on our Grammar page, and I am going to teach it with you. Grammar here just means saying sentences the right way. We will practise water sentences, like "I use water to drink." By the end, you will be able to say clear water sentences all by yourself. You need only your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. There are six little sentence patterns, and we will do them one at a time. Here comes step one. Our first pattern is: I use water to ___. Think of one thing you do with water at home. Then say the whole sentence out loud, and type it to me too. A good answer has all the words, like this one of mine: I use water to cook. Now you try one, and I'll watch.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! Today we are doing our Speaking practice for Wonderful Water. 🌊

Speaking means you say the words out loud with your mouth, not just in your head. We do this so your English gets strong and brave. By the end, you will be able to talk about water all by yourself. You need two things: your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are six little speaking turns. Here comes step one! Step 1: Say this sentence out loud: "I use water to drink."

Say it nice and clear. Then type it here so I know you said it.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we will do Activity 1 together. 🌊

This activity is called "Point and say". You will colour four pictures that use water: a cup, a plant, washing hands, and a pot of soup. We do it so you can name water things out loud in English. By the end, you will be able to point at each picture and say its word clearly. You need your crayons and your activity page. There are four steps — one picture each time. Here comes step one! Find the cup on your page. Colour it any colour you like. Then say the word out loud: "cup."

I am listening — tell me when you have coloured it and said the word.

writing.label: Writing
writing.text:
Hello! Today I am your writing teacher for Unit 8, Wonderful Water. 💧

This page has six little writing jobs. In them you draw, trace, label and write short water sentences. We do this because writing helps your water words stick in your head — and it shows what you know about water. Here is what I expect from you: say your idea out loud first, then draw or write it, and use a capital letter to start a sentence. Neat is good, but brave trying is better! Get ready with paper and a pencil or crayons. Step 1 of 6 — Writing 1: Draw and tell. Draw one way your family uses water at home. Maybe washing hands, drinking, or cooking. Then say out loud: "I use water to ___."

Tell me when your drawing is done, and tell me your sentence too.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Water Games activity. 🌊

In this game we hunt for water and play "float or sink". We do it because playing helps the words stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to name places we find water and say "The ___ floats" or "The ___ sinks."

You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby. Later we will need a bowl of water. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: The Water Hunt. Look around your room or your home. Find ONE place where there is water. It could be a tap, a cup, a puddle, or rain outside. I expect you to tell me the place in a short sentence, like this: "I found water in the cup."

Off you go — tell me what you find!

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Wonderful Water checkpoint. It is a quiz with ten questions about water, weather, floating and sinking. We do it to show what you have learned in this unit — it is like showing off your new skills! You will need your eyes for reading, your ears for listening, and a grown-up nearby to read each question aloud with you. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, choose one answer, and try your best on your own. I will not tell you the answers — but I will cheer you on, and after you finish we can talk about them together. There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: get ready. Sit up nicely, take a breath, and find the first question on your screen. Tell me when you can see question one.

ebooks.label: Books
ebooks.text:
Welcome to our Books page! Today we read our unit story, "The Well in the Village". 📖

It is about a girl called Amal and the water in her village. We read it in small parts, and we talk after each part. This helps you listen well, understand the story, and learn our water words. Here is what I expect from you: read or listen carefully, then answer my question in your own words. Even one or two words is a great answer. You do not need perfect spelling — just tell me what you think. There are 5 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Look at the story title, "The Well in the Village". A well is a deep hole in the ground where people get water. What do you think happens first in this story? Tell me your guess.

overview.label: Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 9, City Places. 🏙️

This first page is our welcome page. It shows what we will learn in this unit: the names of places in a town, the kind people who work there, and the traffic lights that keep us safe. Why do we do it? So you can talk about your own town in English — and say where you go. What I expect from you: say the words out loud, try even when you are not sure, and answer me in short sentences. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are five small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Think about your town. Tell me the name of ONE place you go to. It can be in your language or in English — both are fine.

dictionary.label: Vocabulary
dictionary.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our word time in Unit 9, City Places. 🏙️

In this activity we learn the words for places in our town — like shop, market and library. We do this so you can tell people where you go and what you see. By the end, you will say three new words, know what they mean, and use each one in your own sentence. You need only your voice and your thinking brain. A grown-up can sit with you if one is near. There are 3 steps. Here is step 1. Step 1: Listen to our first word. market — a busy place with many stalls selling fruit and vegetables. Say it out loud with me, slowly: mar-ket. What I expect from you: tell me one thing people can buy at a market.

lecture.label: Video lesson
lecture.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the video lesson in Unit 9: City Places. 🌆

In this lesson we look and listen, then say the words out loud with me. We do it because saying words out loud is how they stick in your mouth and your memory. By the end, you will name places in a town, and you will know that red means stop and green means go. You need just two things: your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. Here is what I expect from you. Say every word out loud, not just in your head. A good try is a loud, clear try — even if it is not perfect. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look around your room and think about your town. Tell me one place you go to in your town. Just one word is fine, like "shop" or "school". What place will you tell me?

reading.label: Reading & story
reading.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to read our unit story together. It is called "A Walk Around Town". In this story, a girl named Amal walks around her town with her mum. We read it to learn the names of town places, like the shop and the library, and to learn what red and green traffic lights mean. Here is what I expect from you: listen carefully, say some words out loud with me, and answer my little questions with your own words. Short answers are perfect. If a grown-up is near you, they can read the story with you too. There are 5 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Look at the title: "A Walk Around Town". Before we read, tell me one place you think Amal will see in her town. What do you think? 😊

comprehension.label: Comprehension
comprehension.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Comprehension. That means we talk about the story "A Walk Around Town" and show that we understood it. We do this so you can listen well, remember, and answer in your own words. By the end, you will answer six little questions about Amal's walk around her town. You need your listening ears and your speaking voice — and your grown-up can sit with you if one is nearby. 🙂

There are six questions, one at a time. Here comes question one. In the story, Amal and Mum come to the big road. The traffic light is red. What does the red light mean? Say it in a short sentence, like "Red means ___." Take your time — there's no rush.

grammar.label: Grammar
grammar.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Grammar page. 😊

Here we learn six little sentence patterns about our town. A pattern is like a train track — you put your own words on it and the sentence rolls out right. Why? So you can tell anyone where you go and what you see, in good English. You need your voice and your thinking brain. A pencil if you like writing. What I expect: say each sentence out loud, in a full sentence, using your own real town. There are six steps. Here comes step one. Step one: "There is a ___."

We say "a" before most places: a shop, a park, a market. But before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say "an": an airport, an office. Now you try. Tell me two places, like this: There is a park. There is an airport.

speaking.label: Speaking
speaking.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Speaking — that means we use our talking voice, not our pencil. 🌟

We will practise saying sentences about places in our town, like the shop, the school and the library. We do this so you can talk about your town in English, out loud and clearly. You need just two things: your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one can sit with you. There are three small steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Say this sentence out loud, nice and clear. There is a shop. I want to hear the whole sentence, not just one word. Say it, then type it here so I know you did it.

writing.label: Writing
writing.text:
Hello! Today I am your writing teacher. 📝
